column4: Goldman Sachs earnings: 'The bad news is out,' analyst says
column10: [Goldman Sachs shares are on the rise despite reporting a Q2 profit miss. Wells Fargo Managing Director Mike Mayo sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to detail his outlook on Goldman Sachs as the banking institution pivots away from consumer services and CEO David Solomon's vision comes into question. Mayo shares his opinion on banking leadership succession plans while stating Goldman Sachs may have had its "second-worst quarter" under Solomon's helm, while excluding the pandemic years.Video Transcript- Goldman Sachs rounding out second quarter earnings season from the big banks and, well, it wasn't pretty. Profits tanked 58%, hit by write downs in the company's consumer and asset management businesses. Embattled CEO, David Solomon, told investors on the conference call, he is confident in his strategy. But should investors be confident in David Solomon?Mike Mayo is Wells Fargo's managing director and head of US large cap bank research. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

column4: Goldman's profits plunged 58% in Q2
column10: [Profits plunged at Goldman Sachs (GS) during the second quarter as the Wall Street giant struggled with its core businesses of dealmaking and trading while taking nearly $1 billion in impairment charges on consumer and commercial real estate holdings.Goldman's investment banking revenue declined 20% from a year ago and trading dropped 14%. That and the impairment charges helped drag earnings down 58%, to $1.2 billion.It was the firm's lowest quarterly profit since early 2020.The results are likely to intensify the scrutiny of CEO David Solomon, who is wrestling with everything from partner unrest to concerns about strategy as he tries to put a costly consumer-banking experiment behind the company.The results this quarter included more costs from that consumer retreat, as Goldman took a $504 million write-down related to the declining value of a specialty lender called GreenSky that Goldman purchased in 2021."This quarter reflects continued strategic execution of our goals," Solomon said in a release. "I remain fully confident that continued execution will enable us to deliver on our through-the-cycle return targets and create significant value for shareholders."Goldman had been downplaying its results ahead of today's release. Its stock closed up roughly 1% after Solomon told analysts he was optimistic about the direction of capital markets and how that might impact his business."It definitely feels better over the course of the last 6 to 8 weeks than it felt earlier in the year," he told the analysts on a conference call.Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. (REUTERS/Brendan McDermid) (Brendan McDermid / reuters)Goldman is the latest of several big banks to report a continued slowdown in investment banking and trading.Revenues from those businesses dropped during the last quarter at Citigroup (C) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) but were up at Bank of America (BAC). At Morgan Stanley (MS), investment banking was flat compared to a year ago while trading revenues were down.Goldman's drops in investment banking and trading were the second-worst among its peers, behind Citigroup.Story continuesEquities trading was one positive, with $3 billion in revenues that were up 1% from the year-ago period. Fixed-income trading was down 26%.Its overall firm revenues of $10.9 billion were also more than analysts expected.'Green shoots?'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Goldman is among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 12,000 jobs since the end of 2022.Bank executives and analysts are still predicting "green shoots" ahead, citing an uptick in announced M&A deals over the second quarter that could mean an improvement during the back half of 2023.Morgan Stanley's CFO Sharon Yeshaya told analysts Tuesday that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. For overall capital markets, "July should be a good indicator for the remainder of the year."Solomon on Wednesday said Goldman's investment banking and trading unit "delivered solid returns in an environment with cyclically low activity levels and we remained #1 in completed M&A – a testament to our world-class client franchise."Retreat from Main StreetGoldman has challenges beyond Wall Street. It is also scaling back its onetime ambitions to become a major presence on Main Street, an effort that started with a savings account and personal loans in 2016 under former CEO Lloyd Blankfein.Read more: The best high-yield savings account rates for July 2023The strategy deepened after Solomon became CEO in 2018, including a credit card partnership with Apple in 2019 and the $1.7 billion purchase of buy-now-pay-later fintech lender GreenSky in 2021.The effort has taken a toll on the firm. Solomon acknowledged earlier this year that a chunk of its consumer business had lost $3 billion since 2020, saying that "we tried to do too much too quickly."The CEO has said Goldman would try to sell GreenSky. The Wall Street Journal has also reported Goldman is now trying to end its partnership with Apple.On Wednesday Goldman said it took a $504 million write-down in the second quarter related to GreenSky. It also took impairments of approximately $485 million related to consolidated real estate investments, some of them office properties.That helped push operating expenses up 12% from the year-ago period.Commercial real estate properties across the US have been under stress over the past year due to rising interest rates from the Federal Reserve.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Investors cheer Wall Street's green shoots as bank executives stay cautious
column10: [By Tatiana Bautzer, Sinéad Carew and Saeed AzharNEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. banking giants reported lackluster results for investment banking in the second quarter, but that has not stopped investors from buying their stocks as a bet on revived dealmaking.Goldman Sachs profit slumped 58% to the lowest in three years, it reported Wednesday, yet its shares climbed more than 1%. While Morgan Stanley's earnings slid 14% over a year before, they beat expectations, sending shares more than 6% higher on Tuesday.So far the signs of revival has not translated into strong investment banking revenue, but markets see a better outlook.“The feeling is that next year looks better than this year and that we may have seen a low point in investment banking revenues,” said Rick Meckler, a partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey.Goldman took $1.4 billion in writedowns in the second quarter tied to its consumer businesses and real estate investments.Still, “investors believe the wind is at their back for investment banking and that it might be cyclical low point," Meckler said, noting the bank's efforts to fix some of its problems.In discussing their earnings, Wall Street executives cited a flurry of initial public offerings as an encouraging sign that activity in capital markets will pick up after months in the doldrums."Big banks have certainly set a positive tone for the start of Q2 reporting season," said Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley's global investment office. "Whether that translates into similar results for the rest of earnings season — and a significant extension and widening of the recent market rally — remains to be seen."But top bankers also cautioned that it was soon to call a lasting recovery, citing a litany of risks facing the economy, including interest rates, inflation and geopolitical tensions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so, and then they start to improve," Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told analysts on a conference call. "We're starting to see that here - it definitely feels better."Story continuesMorgan Stanley's backlog of deals is growing, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are picking up in some industries such as financials and energy, and underwriting trends are improving, Chief Financial Officer Sharon Yeshaya told analysts on a conference call on Tuesday."We expect investment banking to lead the recovery in the next quarter," she said in an interview with Reuters, even though capital markets remained subdued.Bank of America's profits were better than expected in the second quarter, thanks to a surprise gain in its investment banking unit, where net income surged 76%. The lender was buoyed by a slight pickup in equity capital markets and a focus on its middle-market business."We have a very strong and resilient deposit base and we do a lot of moving of money of corporate clients around the world," Alastair Borthwick, BofA's Chief Financial Officer, said on Tuesday. He was referring to the company's transaction services business.At Citigroup, CEO Jane Fraser warned on Friday that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."The company has a strong deal pipeline, but has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A, finance chief Mark Mason said.While some "green shoots" are emerging in the IPO market, JPMorgan Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said on Friday, it is still too early to call it a trend for broader capital markets.(Reporting by Tatiana Bautzer, Sinead Carew and Saeed Azhar in New York, additional reporting by Noor Zainab Hussain in Bengaluru; Editing by Lananh Nguyen and Nick Zieminski)]

column10: [Wall Street is making the case that the the worst is over for Wall Street. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

column4: Goldman's profits plunged 58% in Q2
column10: [Profits plunged at Goldman Sachs (GS) during the second quarter as the Wall Street giant struggled with its core businesses of dealmaking and trading while taking nearly $1 billion in impairment charges on consumer and commercial real estate holdings.Goldman's investment banking revenue declined 20% from a year ago and trading dropped 14%. That and the impairment charges helped drag earnings down 58%, to $1.2 billion.It was the firm's lowest quarterly profit since early 2020.The results are likely to intensify the scrutiny of CEO David Solomon, who is wrestling with everything from partner unrest to concerns about strategy as he tries to put a costly consumer-banking experiment behind the company.The results this quarter included more costs from that consumer retreat, as Goldman took a $504 million write-down related to the declining value of a specialty lender called GreenSky that Goldman purchased in 2021."This quarter reflects continued strategic execution of our goals," Solomon said in a release. "I remain fully confident that continued execution will enable us to deliver on our through-the-cycle return targets and create significant value for shareholders."Goldman had been downplaying its results ahead of today's release. Its stock closed up roughly 1% after Solomon told analysts he was optimistic about the direction of capital markets and how that might impact his business."It definitely feels better over the course of the last 6 to 8 weeks than it felt earlier in the year," he told the analysts on a conference call.Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. (REUTERS/Brendan McDermid) (Brendan McDermid / reuters)Goldman is the latest of several big banks to report a continued slowdown in investment banking and trading.Revenues from those businesses dropped during the last quarter at Citigroup (C) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) but were up at Bank of America (BAC). At Morgan Stanley (MS), investment banking was flat compared to a year ago while trading revenues were down.Goldman's drops in investment banking and trading were the second-worst among its peers, behind Citigroup.Story continuesEquities trading was one positive, with $3 billion in revenues that were up 1% from the year-ago period. Fixed-income trading was down 26%.Its overall firm revenues of $10.9 billion were also more than analysts expected.'Green shoots?'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Goldman is among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 12,000 jobs since the end of 2022.Bank executives and analysts are still predicting "green shoots" ahead, citing an uptick in announced M&A deals over the second quarter that could mean an improvement during the back half of 2023.Morgan Stanley's CFO Sharon Yeshaya told analysts Tuesday that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. For overall capital markets, "July should be a good indicator for the remainder of the year."Solomon on Wednesday said Goldman's investment banking and trading unit "delivered solid returns in an environment with cyclically low activity levels and we remained #1 in completed M&A – a testament to our world-class client franchise."Retreat from Main StreetGoldman has challenges beyond Wall Street. It is also scaling back its onetime ambitions to become a major presence on Main Street, an effort that started with a savings account and personal loans in 2016 under former CEO Lloyd Blankfein.Read more: The best high-yield savings account rates for July 2023The strategy deepened after Solomon became CEO in 2018, including a credit card partnership with Apple in 2019 and the $1.7 billion purchase of buy-now-pay-later fintech lender GreenSky in 2021.The effort has taken a toll on the firm. Solomon acknowledged earlier this year that a chunk of its consumer business had lost $3 billion since 2020, saying that "we tried to do too much too quickly."The CEO has said Goldman would try to sell GreenSky. The Wall Street Journal has also reported Goldman is now trying to end its partnership with Apple.On Wednesday Goldman said it took a $504 million write-down in the second quarter related to GreenSky. It also took impairments of approximately $485 million related to consolidated real estate investments, some of them office properties.That helped push operating expenses up 12% from the year-ago period.Commercial real estate properties across the US have been under stress over the past year due to rising interest rates from the Federal Reserve.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Investors cheer Wall Street's green shoots as bank executives stay cautious
column10: [By Tatiana Bautzer, Sinéad Carew and Saeed AzharNEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. banking giants reported lackluster results for investment banking in the second quarter, but that has not stopped investors from buying their stocks as a bet on revived dealmaking.Goldman Sachs profit slumped 58% to the lowest in three years, it reported Wednesday, yet its shares climbed more than 1%. While Morgan Stanley's earnings slid 14% over a year before, they beat expectations, sending shares more than 6% higher on Tuesday.So far the signs of revival has not translated into strong investment banking revenue, but markets see a better outlook.“The feeling is that next year looks better than this year and that we may have seen a low point in investment banking revenues,” said Rick Meckler, a partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey.Goldman took $1.4 billion in writedowns in the second quarter tied to its consumer businesses and real estate investments.Still, “investors believe the wind is at their back for investment banking and that it might be cyclical low point," Meckler said, noting the bank's efforts to fix some of its problems.In discussing their earnings, Wall Street executives cited a flurry of initial public offerings as an encouraging sign that activity in capital markets will pick up after months in the doldrums."Big banks have certainly set a positive tone for the start of Q2 reporting season," said Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley's global investment office. "Whether that translates into similar results for the rest of earnings season — and a significant extension and widening of the recent market rally — remains to be seen."But top bankers also cautioned that it was soon to call a lasting recovery, citing a litany of risks facing the economy, including interest rates, inflation and geopolitical tensions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so, and then they start to improve," Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told analysts on a conference call. "We're starting to see that here - it definitely feels better."Story continuesMorgan Stanley's backlog of deals is growing, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are picking up in some industries such as financials and energy, and underwriting trends are improving, Chief Financial Officer Sharon Yeshaya told analysts on a conference call on Tuesday."We expect investment banking to lead the recovery in the next quarter," she said in an interview with Reuters, even though capital markets remained subdued.Bank of America's profits were better than expected in the second quarter, thanks to a surprise gain in its investment banking unit, where net income surged 76%. The lender was buoyed by a slight pickup in equity capital markets and a focus on its middle-market business."We have a very strong and resilient deposit base and we do a lot of moving of money of corporate clients around the world," Alastair Borthwick, BofA's Chief Financial Officer, said on Tuesday. He was referring to the company's transaction services business.At Citigroup, CEO Jane Fraser warned on Friday that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."The company has a strong deal pipeline, but has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A, finance chief Mark Mason said.While some "green shoots" are emerging in the IPO market, JPMorgan Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said on Friday, it is still too early to call it a trend for broader capital markets.(Reporting by Tatiana Bautzer, Sinead Carew and Saeed Azhar in New York, additional reporting by Noor Zainab Hussain in Bengaluru; Editing by Lananh Nguyen and Nick Zieminski)]

column4: Wall Street says the worst is over for Wall Street

So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

column4: Goldman's profits plunged 58% in Q2
column10: [Profits plunged at Goldman Sachs (GS) during the second quarter as the Wall Street giant struggled with its core businesses of dealmaking and trading while taking nearly $1 billion in impairment charges on consumer and commercial real estate holdings.Goldman's investment banking revenue declined 20% from a year ago and trading dropped 14%. That and the impairment charges helped drag earnings down 58%, to $1.2 billion.It was the firm's lowest quarterly profit since early 2020.The results are likely to intensify the scrutiny of CEO David Solomon, who is wrestling with everything from partner unrest to concerns about strategy as he tries to put a costly consumer-banking experiment behind the company.The results this quarter included more costs from that consumer retreat, as Goldman took a $504 million write-down related to the declining value of a specialty lender called GreenSky that Goldman purchased in 2021."This quarter reflects continued strategic execution of our goals," Solomon said in a release. "I remain fully confident that continued execution will enable us to deliver on our through-the-cycle return targets and create significant value for shareholders."Goldman had been downplaying its results ahead of today's release. Its stock closed up roughly 1% after Solomon told analysts he was optimistic about the direction of capital markets and how that might impact his business."It definitely feels better over the course of the last 6 to 8 weeks than it felt earlier in the year," he told the analysts on a conference call.Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon. (REUTERS/Brendan McDermid) (Brendan McDermid / reuters)Goldman is the latest of several big banks to report a continued slowdown in investment banking and trading.Revenues from those businesses dropped during the last quarter at Citigroup (C) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) but were up at Bank of America (BAC). At Morgan Stanley (MS), investment banking was flat compared to a year ago while trading revenues were down.Goldman's drops in investment banking and trading were the second-worst among its peers, behind Citigroup.Story continuesEquities trading was one positive, with $3 billion in revenues that were up 1% from the year-ago period. Fixed-income trading was down 26%.Its overall firm revenues of $10.9 billion were also more than analysts expected.'Green shoots?'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Goldman is among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 12,000 jobs since the end of 2022.Bank executives and analysts are still predicting "green shoots" ahead, citing an uptick in announced M&A deals over the second quarter that could mean an improvement during the back half of 2023.Morgan Stanley's CFO Sharon Yeshaya told analysts Tuesday that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. For overall capital markets, "July should be a good indicator for the remainder of the year."Solomon on Wednesday said Goldman's investment banking and trading unit "delivered solid returns in an environment with cyclically low activity levels and we remained #1 in completed M&A – a testament to our world-class client franchise."Retreat from Main StreetGoldman has challenges beyond Wall Street. It is also scaling back its onetime ambitions to become a major presence on Main Street, an effort that started with a savings account and personal loans in 2016 under former CEO Lloyd Blankfein.Read more: The best high-yield savings account rates for July 2023The strategy deepened after Solomon became CEO in 2018, including a credit card partnership with Apple in 2019 and the $1.7 billion purchase of buy-now-pay-later fintech lender GreenSky in 2021.The effort has taken a toll on the firm. Solomon acknowledged earlier this year that a chunk of its consumer business had lost $3 billion since 2020, saying that "we tried to do too much too quickly."The CEO has said Goldman would try to sell GreenSky. The Wall Street Journal has also reported Goldman is now trying to end its partnership with Apple.On Wednesday Goldman said it took a $504 million write-down in the second quarter related to GreenSky. It also took impairments of approximately $485 million related to consolidated real estate investments, some of them office properties.That helped push operating expenses up 12% from the year-ago period.Commercial real estate properties across the US have been under stress over the past year due to rising interest rates from the Federal Reserve.Click here for the latest stock market news and in-depth analysis, including events that move stocksRead the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance]

column4: Investors cheer Wall Street's green shoots as bank executives stay cautious
column10: [By Tatiana Bautzer, Sinéad Carew and Saeed AzharNEW YORK (Reuters) - U.S. banking giants reported lackluster results for investment banking in the second quarter, but that has not stopped investors from buying their stocks as a bet on revived dealmaking.Goldman Sachs profit slumped 58% to the lowest in three years, it reported Wednesday, yet its shares climbed more than 1%. While Morgan Stanley's earnings slid 14% over a year before, they beat expectations, sending shares more than 6% higher on Tuesday.So far the signs of revival has not translated into strong investment banking revenue, but markets see a better outlook.“The feeling is that next year looks better than this year and that we may have seen a low point in investment banking revenues,” said Rick Meckler, a partner at Cherry Lane Investments, a family investment office in New Vernon, New Jersey.Goldman took $1.4 billion in writedowns in the second quarter tied to its consumer businesses and real estate investments.Still, “investors believe the wind is at their back for investment banking and that it might be cyclical low point," Meckler said, noting the bank's efforts to fix some of its problems.In discussing their earnings, Wall Street executives cited a flurry of initial public offerings as an encouraging sign that activity in capital markets will pick up after months in the doldrums."Big banks have certainly set a positive tone for the start of Q2 reporting season," said Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley's global investment office. "Whether that translates into similar results for the rest of earnings season — and a significant extension and widening of the recent market rally — remains to be seen."But top bankers also cautioned that it was soon to call a lasting recovery, citing a litany of risks facing the economy, including interest rates, inflation and geopolitical tensions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so, and then they start to improve," Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon told analysts on a conference call. "We're starting to see that here - it definitely feels better."Story continuesMorgan Stanley's backlog of deals is growing, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) are picking up in some industries such as financials and energy, and underwriting trends are improving, Chief Financial Officer Sharon Yeshaya told analysts on a conference call on Tuesday."We expect investment banking to lead the recovery in the next quarter," she said in an interview with Reuters, even though capital markets remained subdued.Bank of America's profits were better than expected in the second quarter, thanks to a surprise gain in its investment banking unit, where net income surged 76%. The lender was buoyed by a slight pickup in equity capital markets and a focus on its middle-market business."We have a very strong and resilient deposit base and we do a lot of moving of money of corporate clients around the world," Alastair Borthwick, BofA's Chief Financial Officer, said on Tuesday. He was referring to the company's transaction services business.At Citigroup, CEO Jane Fraser warned on Friday that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."The company has a strong deal pipeline, but has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A, finance chief Mark Mason said.While some "green shoots" are emerging in the IPO market, JPMorgan Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said on Friday, it is still too early to call it a trend for broader capital markets.(Reporting by Tatiana Bautzer, Sinead Carew and Saeed Azhar in New York, additional reporting by Noor Zainab Hussain in Bengaluru; Editing by Lananh Nguyen and Nick Zieminski)]

column10: [Bank of America Corporation's (NYSE:BAC) periodic dividend will be increasing on the 29th of September to $0.24, with investors receiving 9.1% more than last year's $0.22. This makes the dividend yield about the same as the industry average at 2.8%. View our latest analysis for Bank of America Bank of America's Dividend Forecasted To Be Well Covered By EarningsWhile it is always good to see a solid dividend yield, we should also consider whether the payment is feasible.Bank of America has established itself as a dividend paying company with over 10 years history of distributing earnings to shareholders. Taking data from its last earnings report, calculating for the company's payout ratio shows 25%, which means that Bank of America would be able to pay its last dividend without pressure on the balance sheet.Looking forward, earnings per share is forecast to fall by 4.1% over the next 3 years. Despite that, analysts estimate the future payout ratio could be 34% over the same time period, which is in a pretty comfortable range.historic-dividendBank of America Has A Solid Track RecordThe company has a sustained record of paying dividends with very little fluctuation. Since 2013, the dividend has gone from $0.04 total annually to $0.88. This works out to be a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of approximately 36% a year over that time. It is good to see that there has been strong dividend growth, and that there haven't been any cuts for a long time.The Dividend Looks Likely To GrowInvestors could be attracted to the stock based on the quality of its payment history. It's encouraging to see that Bank of America has been growing its earnings per share at 13% a year over the past five years. Bank of America definitely has the potential to grow its dividend in the future with earnings on an uptrend and a low payout ratio.Bank of America Looks Like A Great Dividend StockIn summary, it is always positive to see the dividend being increased, and we are particularly pleased with its overall sustainability. The earnings easily cover the company's distributions, and the company is generating plenty of cash. column4: Wall Street says the worst is over for Wall Street
column10: [Wall Street is making the case that the the worst is over for Wall Street. So far investors agree.Top bank executives spent much of this past week pointing to "green shoots" in dealmaking or trading despite in most cases logging another disappointing quarter.Morgan Stanley (MS) CFO Sharon Yeshaya said that "sentiment and activity improved towards the end of the quarter, evidenced by green shoots that emerged across our businesses."Citigroup (C) CFO Mark Mason said "we are seeing green shoots" in the issuance of debt "as clients start to have a greater conviction" about the direction of interest rates.Goldman Sachs (GS) CEO David Solomon said Wednesday that the month of June "was certainly better" than the earlier part of the quarter and that he has noticed more "risk-on sentiment" in July.David M. Solomon, CEO of Goldman Sachs. (REUTERS/Mike Blake) (Mike Blake / reuters)"It definitely feels better over the course of the last six to eight weeks than it felt earlier in the year."That's certainly what investors wanted to hear. Stocks of most big banks rose this past week. Morgan Stanley's stock was up more than 6% on Tuesday after its results were released. Goldman's stock even rose more than 1% Wednesday despite reporting that profits fell by 58%, more than expected.Yet the performance of Wall Street's core businesses were certainly nothing to celebrate across most banks. Trading revenue fell by 22% at Morgan Stanley, 14% at Goldman, 13% at Citigroup, and 10% at JPMorgan Chase. Only Bank of America (BAC) had trading revenue rise, by 7%.The drops were not as much as analysts expected at all but one firm, Morgan Stanley.Investment banking revenues were down by 24% at Citi, 20% at Goldman, and 6% at JPMorgan. They were flat at Morgan Stanley and up 1.6% at Bank of America.The drops at Goldman and Citigroup were worse than expected. For the others, the results beat estimates.'We feel good about where we are'The global slowdown in dealmaking began last year after a boom in 2021, causing firms across Wall Street to slash bonuses and staff. It continued in 2023 as worldwide investment banking revenues for the second quarter fell 52% from a year ago, according to Dealogic.Story continuesGoldman, Morgan Stanley, and Citigroup were among the firms on Wall Street that have made or announced cuts of roughly 20,000 jobs since the end of 2022, resulting in hundreds of millions in severance costs.Goldman spent $260 million through the first half of the year and Citigroup spent $450 million. Morgan Stanley's severance costs were $308 million in the second quarter.Some executives hinted this week that the headcount reductions were likely over."I'm glad we were early in January to work on head count sizing," Solomon said, referring to a decision that month to lay off more than 3,000 workers. But now, "we feel good about where we are."'We will see'Solomon said he is noticing activity picking up in a few spots, citing equity capital markets and mergers and acquisitions."When I go back and I look historically at other periods where the macro environment has created sharp drops in investment banking activity, they tend to last for a year or so and then they start to improve," the CEO said. "And so I think we're starting to see that here. It definitely feels better."Goldman, he added, doesn't have to go back to the boom period of 2021 to see "material uplift."At Morgan Stanley, Yeshaya said the firm's backlog of deals is on the rise and M&A activity is picking up in energy and financials.Mason, at Citigoup, cited a "healthy" M&A pipeline "which we would expect to unlock as the sentiment continues to improve." Still the company has "more work to do" on equity capital markets and M&A.His boss, CEO Jane Fraser, also sounded a cautious note. In a release she said that "the long-awaited rebound in investment banking has yet to materialize."Then she told analysts "corporates are pretty cautious," citing the prospect of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike, tensions with China, and concerns about limited economic growth.Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser. "I think they now seem to accept the current environment is the new normal and are beginning to position themselves globally."JPMorgan CFO Jeremy Barnum said investment banking was better than expected in June, but cautioned analysts on Friday that it was "too early" to label it a trend."We will see," he said. column4: Goldman Sachs earnings: 'The bad news is out,' analyst says
column10: [Goldman Sachs shares are on the rise despite reporting a Q2 profit miss. Wells Fargo Managing Director Mike Mayo sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to detail his outlook on Goldman Sachs as the banking institution pivots away from consumer services and CEO David Solomon's vision comes into question. Mayo shares his opinion on banking leadership succession plans while stating Goldman Sachs may have had its "second-worst quarter" under Solomon's helm, while excluding the pandemic years.Video Transcript- Goldman Sachs rounding out second quarter earnings season from the big banks and, well, it wasn't pretty. Profits tanked 58%, hit by write downs in the company's consumer and asset management businesses. Embattled CEO, David Solomon, told investors on the conference call, he is confident in his strategy. But should investors be confident in David Solomon?Mike Mayo is Wells Fargo's managing director and head of US large cap bank research. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

column4: Fed set to propose new banking capital requirements, 'Basel III endgame'
column10: [Fed officials are set to unveil an overhaul of banking capital requirements, known as the "Basel III endgame," this week. American Banker Staff Writer Kyle Campbell sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to explain the ways in which these guidelines will mitigate risk differently for various forms of credit lending. Campbell describes how these new guidelines will impact certain larger, institutional banks, while examining the exposure regional banks may have to commercial real estate.Video Transcript- All right. On Thursday, just one day after the FOMC's latest interest rate decision, Federal Reserve will unveil a proposal for new bank capital requirements. The proposed rule would also lower the threshold for qualifying banks, meaning smaller institutions will face a new host of demands previously avoided.Fed vice chair for supervision, Michael Barr, outlined a sweeping plan to overhaul bank oversight requirements earlier this month. The proposal, set to come out Thursday, will offer more specifics on just how significant those changes could be.Joining us now with the latest is Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker. Kyle, good to see you here. I talked to Brian Moynihan, CEO of Bank of America, about this. He really took a-- I would say, a hard line view of this. This could really be impactful to the economy. What have you been hearing from sources?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, I mean, that's the big concern, right. Banks have been looking forward to this proposal for a long time now. Since 2017 is when the Basel III, they call it endgame, was first finalized, sort of, internationally, and now we're implementing that.Where this is-- what we're going to see on Thursday is just how that's going to impact the economy because we're going to find out which particular activities are going to be given which sort of risk weights under the new framework. So if, let's say, auto lending comes with a much heavier capital penalty, than a lot of banks are sort of forecasting with their internal models currently. It's going to make that type of financing more expensive, essentially.Story continuesAnd there is a view that as capital overall increases, it's just going to have a broader, sort of, tightening impact on the availability of credit broadly in the economy.- Is it really? Or is it just that their margins are going to get smaller? Or both, right?KYLE CAMPBELL: I think it's probably a bit of both but that's a great question. And certainly, consumer advocates are saying, well, look, the way that capital is raised is it's just hurting the bottom line for executives. You just have to retained earnings and you lose that sort of ROE, return on equity, that is what sort of fuels bank profits.So it's certainly going to result in less profitability, at least for some period of time. And again, how that actually impacts the availability of credit to the average person is going to really, I think-- I don't think it's particularly useful to try to forecast the overall picture, but you can get a good sense of how individual banks are going to be impacted by this once we see the specifics on Thursday.- For those banks, let's say a Wells Fargo, that have been struggling for some time, what does this mean for the struggling banks like a Wells Fargo?KYLE CAMPBELL: Wells Fargo, it'll be interesting. I mean, obviously if-- I mean, they've started to sort of move away from mortgages, which is one area where there's going to be a lot of focus. What happens to mortgages. You know, how does it get treated under the capital rules.I mean-- I think that where it's going to be more impactful than at Wells Fargo-- I mean, certainly they're going to be hit to some degree. But I think it's really going to be most impactful on the sort of mid-size banks, if you will. The ones that were in that sort of 100 billion to 250 billion asset range, that are now going to be facing these capital-- these sort of risk capital requirements for the first time.I think the large banks sort of know how to deal with these sort of requirements. And I don't think that a Wells Fargo is going to be as impacted, on a relative basis, as some of the smaller banks.- Let's turn to another issue that the market's been paying a lot of attention to, and that's commercial real estate and the risks associated with commercial real estate. In these earnings reports that we've gotten from banks, several of them announced steps to anticipate losses. To put aside money for losses, potential losses in commercial real estate.Wells Fargo, for example, boosted its allowance for credit losses. So where are we in that sort of situation?KYLE CAMPBELL: Yeah, that's a great question. And certainly, regulators are very focused on commercial real estate, giving some strong warnings to banks to do things like set aside losses and sort of avoid getting new exposures where you can avoid it.And that actually kind of compounds the issue because a lot of these-- I mean, certainly with offices, we know, the ones that are vacant, not getting people in, and that's sort of a whole issue unto itself. But there are some assets where they're kind of performing relatively well but they're going to need some kind of a recapitalization in order to remain viable and not end up as a foreclosure. And in order to do that, you need banks to sort come to the table.So I think what we're going to be looking for is who's going to move first. Are we going to see some of these sort of big capital equity investors, private equity funds, start to come in and say, hey, we're going to move in in a higher equity basis? Or are we going to see some banks say, hey, actually, we're going to be willing to back some of these recap-type strategies through lending?- Is this a potentially destabilizing event for the banking sector?KYLE CAMPBELL: I wouldn't think so.- I'm trying to compare it to what happened earlier this year.KYLE CAMPBELL: Right. Yeah. I mean, I think you're going to see some serious stress. And I wouldn't be surprised if at specific banks, you see some possible failures. I mean, you don't want to throw that term around too lightly. But yeah, it's possible that some banks could either have to be sold or go through some sort of an M&A activity to sort of right the ship here.I wouldn't expect it to get to a level where we're needing to see serious intervention by the government because they're sort of very well aware of what's going on in real time. But these things can snowball pretty quickly. So yeah, it could be something to watch for sure.- Yeah, most definitely. Kyle, thanks for coming in. Good to see you. Kyle Campbell, staff writer at American Banker, covering some various areas of risks for us.]

column4: Bank of America Awards $1M Grant to National Juneteenth Museum
column10: [New legacy institution will educate visitors on the past, create growth in the present and inspire future generations.FORT WORTH, Texas, July 25, 2023 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Juneteenth Museum and Bank of America today announced a foundational gift to support the first-of-its-kind museum. Selected to be built in Fort Worth, the city is a hub for arts and culture institutions and celebration, and the city's history is closely tied to its identity today. Honoring Fort Worth's past by investing in its future, Bank of America is awarding a $1M grant for the development of the National Juneteenth Museum ecosystem.Ariel view of The National Juneteenth Museum"The National Juneteenth Museum will be a social and economic anchor in Fort Worth that will serve as a catalyst for community education and growth. The bank's foundational support acknowledges the significant role Juneteenth plays in our city's history and is another demonstration of our commitment to advance economic opportunity and racial equality," said Mike Pavell, Bank of America Fort Worth President. "We're excited to work with the National Juneteenth Museum to revitalize the local community and create a new legacy institution."Fostering a true ecosystem for economic and cultural development, the National Juneteenth Museum will feature far more than its collection of artifacts. The 50,000-square-foot center will host guest lectures, community events and performances in its 250-seat amphitheater, bring families together through the on-site food hall and grand green space, and launch big ideas into reality in its business incubator."The predominantly African American neighborhood surrounding the museum has helped shape Fort Worth for generations. I'm encouraged to see Bank of America helping breathe life into the Historic Southside through intentional investment in cultural education and preservation. Residents, visitors and local businesses will be able to witness the impact of Bank of America's gift, supporting a space where generational wealth, health and tradition will have a collaborative space to flourish," said Jarred Howard, CEO of the National Juneteenth Museum.Story continues"The National Juneteenth Museum personifies many of the core values we uphold at Bank of America. From supporting diverse entrepreneurs and small business development, to mobilizing the power of the arts to educate and enrich our societies, we look forward to working together to unite our community and create greater cultural understanding. This partnership is a point of pride for Bank of America not only here in Fort Worth, but in every corner of our national footprint," added Pavell.The museum's targeted opening date is June 19, 2025.
